# INTRODUCTION

This chapter identifies the problem that the study addresses and defines the objectives of a solution. It describes why the problem matters, what the study asks and aims to achieve, the frameworks behind the study, and the boundaries and significance of the study.

## Introduction to the Study

According to the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration [PAGASA, -@pagasa2026cyclone], about eight or nine tropical cyclones cross the Philippines each year. During these tropical cyclones, Filipinos use social media to warn others, report damage, and ask for help [@ermino2022urgency; @caoile2025urdaneta]. The sheer volume of posts can make useful information difficult and time-consuming for responders to find [@somido2023actionable]. Natural language processing (NLP), in which computers process human language, can help automate this work [@lewis2025tapping]. Humanitarian classification assigns each post a category by the kind of report [@alam2021humaid], and named entity recognition (NER) identifies entities in the post, such as places and requests for aid [@ali2026humaidner]. A multi-task model, trained on both tasks at once, can outperform single-task models, which are each trained on one task alone, because what it learns for one task can help the other [@wang2021transformer]. However, learning one task can also interfere with learning the other, a problem known as negative transfer [@royer2023scalarization]. Multi-task optimizers aim to reduce this problem by controlling how the tasks influence the model during training [@xin2022mtohelp]. Studies disagree on whether specialized multi-task optimizers outperform equal weighting, which simply gives both tasks the same weight, and the gains reported for many specialized multi-task optimizers come at the cost of more training time and memory [@kurin2022unitary; @gama2026uniform]. Although code-switching between Tagalog and English, known as Taglish, is very common in the Philippines [@herrera2022tweettaglish], none of the studies reviewed provides a dataset in which the same Taglish posts are annotated for both tasks or compares multi-task optimizers on such posts. This study therefore builds a dataset of Taglish typhoon posts annotated for both tasks and benchmarks 13 multi-task optimizers on negative transfer and training cost. The final model uses the optimizer selected based on negative transfer and is compared with single-task models. The study contributes the dataset, the final model, and evidence on how much these optimizers reduce negative transfer and at what training cost.

## Background of the Study

The Philippines has the highest disaster risk among 193 countries, and part of this risk comes from its high exposure to weather-related extremes [@bundnis2025worldriskreport]. During disasters, social media posts can give responders the firsthand information they need to respond quickly, but their sheer volume can make this information difficult and time-consuming to find [@somido2023actionable]. Studies have therefore used NLP to classify these posts and extract their most relevant information automatically [@mcdaniel2024zeroshot]. Humanitarian classification tells responders what kind of report a post is, and NER tells them where help is needed and what resources are sought [@ali2026humaidner].

Several Philippine studies have applied NLP to disaster posts. @ermino2022urgency classified typhoon posts by urgency, and @somido2023actionable classified disaster posts by whether they were informative. @yute2021satellite used NER to extract the locations mentioned in posts about the 2020 Taal Volcano eruption. @caoile2025urdaneta used a large language model (LLM) to detect the sentiment, urgency, and intent of Facebook comments in Urdaneta City and to extract entities such as place names.

A multi-task model could provide both kinds of information that responders need. It can share one pretrained transformer encoder such as BERT between the two tasks and give each task its own output layer [@wang2021transformer; @gama2026uniform]. Because the encoder has already learned from large amounts of text, the model can be fine-tuned on a relatively small dataset annotated for both tasks [@bucher2024finetuned].

However, multi-task models can also perform worse on a task than single-task models, a problem known as negative transfer [@kurin2022unitary; @royer2023scalarization]. This problem has been reported when classification and NER are trained together. In @zhu2025prefinetuning, an encoder trained on both tasks at once performed slightly worse on each task than encoders trained on one task, because the tasks needed it to represent tokens in conflicting ways. In @ali2026humaidner, classification performance fell as training continued when both tasks had fixed weights, which the authors attributed to NER providing a training signal for every token while classification provides only one for the whole post.

Studies disagree on whether specialized multi-task optimizers reduce negative transfer better than equal weighting. Specialized multi-task optimizers adjust how strongly each task influences the model as training proceeds, whereas equal weighting gives both tasks the same weight throughout training [@gama2026uniform]. When tested against equal weighting [@kurin2022unitary] or fixed task weights chosen by comparing several weight settings [@xin2022mtohelp], specialized multi-task optimizers performed no better, despite the extra training time and memory that many of them need. @gama2026uniform found that specialized multi-task optimizers matched equal weighting when the two tasks produced similar training signals and outperformed equal weighting on more complex problems.

The studies reviewed leave two gaps. First, none of them provides a dataset in which the same Taglish posts are annotated for both humanitarian classification and NER. Such a dataset allows both outputs of a multi-task model to be evaluated on the same posts. @ali2026humaidner created a dataset of this kind for English disaster posts by adding NER annotations to posts that already had humanitarian categories [@alam2021humaid]. This gap reflects a wider shortage, since Tagalog and Taglish are low-resource languages in NLP, with fewer annotated datasets than languages such as English [@cruz2022tagalog; @herrera2022tweettaglish]. Second, none of them compares multi-task optimizers for humanitarian classification and NER on Taglish posts, on either negative transfer or training cost. Because the findings on multi-task optimizers disagree and depend on the problem [@gama2026uniform], the optimizer that best reduces negative transfer cannot be known in advance and has to be found through such a comparison.

## Statement of the Problem

This study aims to develop a dataset and a multi-task model for humanitarian classification and NER of Taglish typhoon posts, and to compare multi-task optimizers for this model in negative transfer and training cost. Specifically, it answers four research questions.

1. What F1-scores do single-task models achieve for humanitarian classification and for NER on Taglish typhoon posts? (Baseline Analysis)

2. How can a dataset and a multi-task model be designed for humanitarian classification and NER of Taglish typhoon posts? (Design and Artifact Creation)

3. How do the 13 multi-task optimizers compare in negative transfer, training time, and peak memory? (Empirical Benchmarking)

4. How does the final multi-task model compare with the single-task models in F1-score, training time, and peak memory? (Comparative Validation)

## Objectives

The general objective is to develop a dataset and a multi-task model for humanitarian classification and NER of Taglish typhoon posts, and to compare multi-task optimizers for this model in negative transfer and training cost. Specifically, the study pursues four objectives.

1. To measure the F1-scores of single-task models for humanitarian classification and for NER on Taglish typhoon posts. (Baseline Analysis)

2. To design and build a dataset and a multi-task model for humanitarian classification and NER of Taglish typhoon posts. (Design and Artifact Creation)

3. To compare the 13 multi-task optimizers in negative transfer, training time, and peak memory. (Empirical Benchmarking)

4. To compare the final multi-task model with the single-task models in F1-score, training time, and peak memory. (Comparative Validation)

## Hypotheses

The study tests the following null and alternative hypotheses for each of the two tasks, humanitarian classification and NER.

**Null hypothesis ($H_0$).** The mean F1-score across training runs of the final multi-task model is the same as that of the single-task model for that task.

**Alternative hypothesis ($H_1$).** The mean F1-score across training runs of the final multi-task model differs from that of the single-task model for that task.

## Theoretical Framework

This study draws on the view of multi-task learning as inductive transfer, in which related tasks share a representation so that what is learned for one task carries over to the others [@caruana1997multitask]. When this transfer helps a task, it is called positive transfer, and when learning one task interferes with learning the other, it is called negative transfer [@royer2023scalarization]. Both have been observed, with multi-task models performing better than single-task models in one study [@wang2021transformer] and worse in another [@zhu2025prefinetuning]. In this study, both tasks share the pretrained transformer encoder, so the final multi-task model may score higher or lower than a single-task model on each task. The hypotheses therefore test for a difference in F1-score in either direction.

## Conceptual Framework

The conceptual framework of this study consists of the research paradigm in @fig-research-paradigm and the design of the multi-task model in @fig-artifact. It centers on two comparisons, one among the 13 multi-task optimizers and one between the final multi-task model and the single-task models.

![Research Paradigm](figures/fig-1-1-research-paradigm.pdf){#fig-research-paradigm}

@fig-research-paradigm follows the Input-Process-Output (IPO) model. The inputs are the Taglish posts, the categories of HumAID and the entity types of HUMAID-NER, the pretrained transformer encoder, the 13 multi-task optimizers, and the laptop used for training. The process has four steps, each answering one research question. The study first designs and builds the dataset and the multi-task model (RQ2) and then trains a single-task model for each task to measure the baseline F1-scores (RQ1). It then benchmarks the 13 multi-task optimizers and selects the optimizer of the final model based on negative transfer (RQ3). Finally, it compares the final model with the single-task models (RQ4). The outputs are the dataset, the final multi-task model, and the comparison of the 13 multi-task optimizers.

![Multi-Task Model](figures/fig-1-2-artifact.pdf){#fig-artifact}

@fig-artifact shows how the multi-task model processes an example post. Both tasks share one pretrained transformer encoder, which reads the post once. The classification head uses the output for the whole post and assigns it a humanitarian category, while the NER head uses the output for each token and identifies the named entities. The dashed lines show the steps that occur only during training, in which the multi-task optimizer decides how the errors of the two tasks update the shared encoder so that the model improves on both tasks.

## Scope, Limitations, and Delimitations

### Scope of the Study

The study covers Taglish posts on X, formerly Twitter, about the tropical cyclones of January to November 2026. The posts come from one day before to three days after the period each tropical cyclone spent within the Philippine Area of Responsibility, the area that PAGASA monitors for tropical cyclones, based on the dates in the preliminary reports of PAGASA [-@pagasa2026prelim]. The dataset consists of about 2,500 posts, each annotated with one of the ten humanitarian categories of HumAID [@alam2021humaid] and with the ten entity types of HUMAID-NER [@ali2026humaidner].

The study trains two single-task models, one for each task, and a multi-task model that performs both tasks. All models are built on one pretrained transformer encoder, SEA-LION-ModernBERT-300M, which was trained on 13 languages, including English and Filipino [@aisingapore2026sealion], and the multi-task model shares this encoder between the two tasks. The multi-task model is trained with each of 13 existing multi-task optimizers reviewed in Section 2.2, which gives 13 candidate models from which the final model is selected based on negative transfer.

The study measures the agreement between annotators on the labels. For every model, it measures the F1-score on each task, the training time, and the peak memory, which is the largest amount of GPU memory used during training.

The study builds a prototype web application that performs humanitarian classification and NER on posts with the final model, and tests whether each of its functions works.

### Limitations of the Study

The dataset may not fully represent Taglish posts about tropical cyclones, and some of its entity annotations may be wrong. The posts come only from users of X, who may not represent everyone affected by tropical cyclones. X also does not reliably show the region of a user, so the dataset may not represent the Taglish of every region equally. The size of about 2,500 posts is set by annotation capacity rather than by what the models need, so the dataset may be too small, and Section 3.7 checks whether it is large enough with a learning curve. Rare humanitarian categories may also have too few test posts for precise F1-scores. The entity spans are annotated automatically by GLiNER and are not checked by the annotators (Section 3.4), so the F1-scores for NER measure agreement with these annotations rather than with human annotations. For the humanitarian categories, the disagreements that remain after discussion are decided by one adjudicator, and no agreement measure checks these decisions.

The experiments are limited by the number of training runs and by the laptop used for training. Each candidate model is trained only three times, so the statistical tests may fail to detect small differences between an optimizer and equal weighting, and a difference that is not significant does not show that the two perform the same (Section 3.6). The training time and peak memory may differ on computers other than the laptop used. The F1-scores may also be lower than if every layer of the encoder were trained, because the embedding layer is frozen to fit the 8 GB of GPU memory of the laptop (Section 3.5).

The findings may not hold beyond the conditions of the study. They come from the tropical cyclones of January to November 2026 and may not hold for tropical cyclones of other years. The comparison of the optimizers is based on one pair of tasks and one pretrained transformer encoder, and because the findings on multi-task optimizers depend on the problem [@gama2026uniform], the best optimizer may differ for other tasks or encoders.

### Delimitations of the Study

The dataset covers only Taglish posts on X about the tropical cyclones of January to November 2026. Posts from Facebook and other platforms are excluded. X allows posts collected through its API to be stored, provided that posts later deleted on X are also deleted [@x2026devpolicy], and earlier Philippine and international disaster datasets also use posts from Twitter [@ermino2022urgency; @somido2023actionable; @alam2021humaid]. Other Philippine languages, such as Cebuano and Waray, are excluded because results from a mix of languages would not show whether the model works the same way in each language. Other hazards, such as earthquakes and volcanic eruptions, are excluded because tropical cyclones alone cross the Philippines about eight or nine times a year [PAGASA, -@pagasa2026cyclone], which gives several events in a single year. Earlier years are excluded because training depends on the number of annotated posts rather than the number of years, and the study does not measure how Taglish changes over time. December is excluded because the posts must be collected before annotation begins that month. Images, video, and audio are excluded because both tasks are defined on text.

The study covers only humanitarian classification and NER. Other tasks, such as sentiment analysis, urgency detection, and the classification of hazard types, are excluded because adding tasks would change how the tasks interfere with one another and make differences in negative transfer harder to attribute to the optimizers. The model therefore does not rate how urgent a request is or identify the type of hazard in a post. It also does not translate posts into English, since its pretrained transformer encoder was trained on both English and Filipino [@aisingapore2026sealion]. Whether a post is true is not verified, because checking a claim requires sources outside the post, such as official reports.

The experiments compare 13 existing multi-task optimizers on one pretrained transformer encoder and one laptop. The study compares these optimizers rather than creating a new one, and other existing optimizers are excluded to keep the number of training runs feasible. Other encoders are excluded because they would add a variable besides the optimizer. Other computers are excluded so that the training time and peak memory of every optimizer are measured under the same conditions. The models are evaluated only on the test posts of the study, because other disaster datasets, such as the English dataset of HUMAID-NER [@ali2026humaidner], differ in language and annotation. The final model is also not compared with LLMs, such as GPT, which differ from it in size, training, and cost. Earlier studies have already made this comparison for classification [@bucher2024finetuned; @mcdaniel2024zeroshot].

The study does not cover the use of the final model or the prototype in practice. Use during actual disasters and usability testing with staff of local disaster risk reduction and management offices are excluded, because the research questions concern how the model is designed, trained, and evaluated. The final model and the prototype are also not maintained after the study. Instead, the final model, the code, and the post IDs of the dataset are released on GitHub so that other researchers can retrain the model on posts from new tropical cyclones.

## Significance of the Study

The study mainly benefits researchers in NLP and in crisis informatics, the field that studies how information from social media can support disaster response. These researchers gain a dataset of Taglish typhoon posts annotated for both humanitarian classification and NER, which none of the studies reviewed provides, to train and evaluate models for both tasks.

Researchers in multi-task learning gain evidence on how much specialized multi-task optimizers reduce negative transfer compared with equal weighting on Taglish posts, and at what training cost. Whether these optimizers perform better than equal weighting is still debated, and a result on one dataset and set of tasks may not hold on another [@kurin2022unitary; @xin2022mtohelp; @gama2026uniform]. Evidence from humanitarian classification and NER of Taglish posts therefore adds a case that the earlier comparisons did not cover.

Local disaster risk reduction and management offices gain one model that classifies Taglish posts and extracts their key details. The comparison of the final model with the single-task models shows what an office would gain or give up in F1-score by using one model instead of two. The prototype demonstrates how office staff could use the model to find requests for rescue and relief more quickly among the many posts made during a disaster.

Future researchers who continue this work can retrain or extend the final model, because the study releases the final model, the code, the annotation guidelines, and the post IDs of the dataset on GitHub. They can retrain the final model on posts from new tropical cyclones, build similar datasets for other Philippine languages, or add tasks such as urgency detection. The dataset is shared as post IDs rather than the posts themselves, as the developer policy of X requires [@x2026devpolicy].

## Definitions of Terms

The following terms are defined as they are used in this study.

**Candidate model**: One of the 13 multi-task models, each trained with a different multi-task optimizer, from which the final model is selected.

**Equal weighting**: The multi-task optimizer that adds the losses of the tasks with the same weight throughout training [@kurin2022unitary]. In this study, it is the reference against which the other 12 optimizers are compared.

**F1-score**: A score from 0 to 1 that combines precision, the share of predictions that are correct, and recall, the share of correct answers that a model finds. In this study, humanitarian classification is scored with macro-F1, the mean of the F1-scores of all categories, and NER with span-level micro-F1, which counts an entity as correct only when both its boundaries and its type match the annotation [@ali2026humaidner].

**Final model**: The candidate model trained with the multi-task optimizer selected based on negative transfer, which is compared with the single-task models.

**Humanitarian classification**: The task of assigning a post one category that names the kind of humanitarian information it reports [@alam2021humaid]. In this study, each post receives one of the ten categories of HumAID, such as requests or urgent needs.

**Inter-annotator agreement**: The degree to which annotators who annotate the same items independently give the same annotations. In this study, it is measured with Cohen's kappa between the two annotators on the humanitarian categories [@cohen1960coefficient].

**Multi-task model**: A model trained on several tasks together that shares a representation across them [@caruana1997multitask]. In this study, it is one pretrained transformer encoder shared by a task head for humanitarian classification and a task head for NER.

**Multi-task optimizer**: A method that decides how the training signals of the tasks are combined into one update of a multi-task model [@lin2023libmtl]. The study compares 13 multi-task optimizers.

**Named entity recognition (NER)**: The task of finding the words or phrases in a text that name specific details and assigning each an entity type. In this study, the posts are annotated with the ten entity types of HUMAID-NER, such as locations and requests [@ali2026humaidner].

**Negative transfer**: A drop in performance on a task when it is trained together with another task, compared with training it alone [@royer2023scalarization]. In this study, it is a lower F1-score of a candidate model on a task than that of the single-task model for that task, and a higher F1-score is positive transfer.

**Peak memory**: The largest amount of GPU memory allocated during one training run.

**Post**: A message published on social media. In this study, it is a public post on X, which the title calls a Tweet, the name used when X was called Twitter.

**Pretrained transformer encoder**: A language model trained on large amounts of text before it is used for a task, which converts each token of a text into numbers that task heads can use. In this study, it is SEA-LION-ModernBERT-300M, which was trained on 13 languages, including English and Filipino [@aisingapore2026sealion].

**Single-task model**: A model trained on one task only. In this study, each single-task model uses the same pretrained transformer encoder as the multi-task model with one task head, and its F1-score is the baseline for measuring negative transfer on that task.

**Specialized multi-task optimizer**: A multi-task optimizer that adjusts how strongly each task influences the model as training proceeds [@gama2026uniform]. In this study, these are the 11 of the 13 optimizers that do not keep the task weights fixed.

**Taglish**: Code-switching between Tagalog and English in the same text [@herrera2022tweettaglish]. In this study, a post is Taglish when it has at least one English word and one Tagalog word.

**Task head**: The part of a multi-task or single-task model that makes the predictions for one task from the output of the pretrained transformer encoder.

**Token**: A word or part of a word that the pretrained transformer encoder reads as one unit.

**Training cost**: The training time and peak memory of a model. Training time is the wall-clock time of the training steps of one run.

**Typhoon**: In the title, any tropical cyclone, a rotating storm that forms over warm ocean water. In this study, it covers all tropical cyclones that entered the Philippine Area of Responsibility from January to November 2026.
